title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
authors: Steven Abel, Michael Spannowsky, Simon Williams
abstract: Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.
summary: This work develops a framework to simulate resonant fermion scattering using a hybrid quantum-computing approach on a photonic platform. By modeling the Yukawa theory, the authors use tensor networks and real-time evolution to track energy and entanglement transfer during collisions. The results confirm that the simulation accurately captures key physical phenomena, establishing a valuable benchmark for future quantum hardware applications in particle physics.
main_problem: The study aims to develop and test a concrete benchmark for simulating resonant scattering dynamics, specifically fermion-antifermion collisions, using hybrid quantum-computing frameworks.
main_result: The simulations successfully reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate and exhibit energy scans consistent with Breit-Wigner behavior, validating the approach for probing particle-resonance dynamics.
method: The research combines theoretical modeling of lattice Yukawa theory with numerical simulations (MPS) and proposes a physical implementation using photonic quantum computing architectures.
model_or_system: The system is based on $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory, coupling fermions (encoded in qubits) to a scalar field (encoded in qumodes). The platform is a hybrid CV-DV architecture utilizing photonic qubits.
key_observables: Time-dependent correlators, localized scalar excitation ($\Delta n_{loc}$), bipartite entanglement entropy ($\Delta S$), and the resonance peak in the scattering cross-section.
important_parameters: The coupling constant ($g$), fermion mass ($m_f$), and scalar mass ($m_\phi$) are key parameters, with resonance behavior being highly dependent on these values.
main_assumptions: The study is currently limited to a finite-lattice simulation, and full hardware implementation requires advanced initial state preparation techniques.

paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical model (Yukawa theory), details the hybrid quantum encoding (qubits/qumodes), presents the simulation methodology (MPS, real-time evolution), and validates the results by comparing measured observables (correlators, energy flow) against analytical predictions.
why_interesting: It provides a direct, measurable benchmark for quantum hardware by linking fundamental particle physics (scattering) to observable quantum information metrics (entanglement, energy transfer).
